co_shelf_road.blurb: Shelf Road is a limestone sport-climbing destination in the dry country north of Cañon City, Colorado. Nearly all of the climbing is bolted single-pitch sport, with a smaller helping of trad and a few boulders. The grade spread leans hard: the bulk sits between 5.10 and 5.12, though there is a solid supply of 5.7 to 5.9 and a thin top end into 5.13. The stone is hard, often sharp, and features pockets, flakes and sustained crimping on near-vertical walls. Winters are mild, which draws climbers when higher Colorado is snowed in, while summers run hot and shade becomes the deciding factor. The Bank is the largest sector and suits newer leaders, The Gallery is steeper and harder, Cactus Cliff faces south and takes the sun, and Sand Gulch offers continuous vertical panels.

ny_the_gunks.blurb: The Gunks, the Shawangunk Ridge in southeastern New York, are among the best-known cliff-climbing areas in the country. The rock is hard quartz conglomerate, and its cracks run horizontally, so protection is placed sideways and most routes are traditional. There are few bolts and essentially no sport climbing. Cliffs reach roughly 250 to 300 feet, with routes of one to three pitches that feature roofs, jugs, traverses and technical faces. Grades run from easy trad up through 5.12, with the greatest concentration between 5.7 and 5.11, and ratings have a stiff reputation. Bouldering and top-roping add variety. The Trapps is the longest and busiest cliff, the Near Trapps sits beside it, Peterskill is a quieter single-pitch and bouldering venue, and Millbrook is more remote. Autumn is prime season; summers are hot and humid, and winter allows few days on rock.

ma_lynn_woods.blurb: Lynn Woods is a wooded municipal reservation just north of Boston, with ponds and trails, and it is a bouldering area first and foremost. Granite boulders are scattered through the forest, and a small number of top-rope, trad and sport lines exist on the side. The rock is coarse New England granite that grips well but wears skin on long sessions. Problems cover technical slabs, crimpy faces, steep overhangs and powerful lines. Grades are friendly to most climbers, with plenty from V0 to V6 and the heaviest concentration around V2 to V5, and only a handful beyond V8. It is spread over many named sub-areas, such as Stone Tower, Weetamoo, Bow Ridge and the Mt. Spickett and Goliath Rock zone, so a day here usually means hiking between clusters.

ok_wichita_mountains_wildlife_refuge.blurb: The Wichita Mountains rise as steep, rocky granite hills above mixed-grass prairie in southwestern Oklahoma, near Lawton, and the refuge here is one of the main climbing destinations of the southern plains. Bouldering is the biggest part, with trad second and a modest amount of sport and top-rope. Rock is granite, with wilderness-feeling multi-pitch routes and large boulders offering good exposure. Trad and sport routes span roughly 5.5 up to the low 5.13s, with most of the climbing from 5.6 to 5.12, while boulder problems are mostly V0 to V5 with some harder. The main concentrations are Charon's Gardens, Mount Scott and The Narrows, along with Dog Run Hollow and the Meadows. Routes can be technical and test even experienced climbers.

ut_northern_wasatch.blurb: The Northern Wasatch covers the climbing north of Salt Lake City, centered on Logan and Cache Valley and on Ogden. Sport routes make up about half of the climbing, followed by bouldering and trad, with a little ice and mixed. Logan Canyon holds limestone, with hundreds of single-pitch sport routes for beginners through advanced climbers. Ogden is built mostly on quartzite and splits fairly evenly among sport, trad and bouldering, with sport walls above the city and a foothill boulder field. Grades range widely: sport and trad cluster from 5.9 to 5.12, with a real number of 5.13s, plus boulder problems from easy to hard. Cache Valley is mostly sport and bouldering; Ogden is more mixed. Winter outdoors is a tough time to climb here.

ca_north_san_diego_county.blurb: North San Diego County is dominated by bouldering, with a good amount of trad and top-rope and a smaller supply of sport. The rock is granitic throughout, and Mount Woodson, between Poway and Ramona, is the best-known area, with compact granodiorite. The granite there is fine-grained, sharp and grippy, and climbing leans toward crimps, finger cracks, slabs and delicate footwork, with some problems edging toward highball. Poway Crags offers vertical sport lines on fine-grained granite. Boulder grades run mainly V0 to V5 with a decent tail to V10 and beyond; roped climbs sit mostly at 5.7 to 5.12. Climbing is possible all year, but summer heat makes many crags unpleasant, and spring and fall are best at Woodson. Lake Ramona and Mount Gower are among the other sub-areas.
